clue.text: It gives us pause, in a manner of speaking

definitions.text: It gives us pause, in a manner of speaking

parts.words: It gives us pause, in a manner of speaking
parts.note: a punctuation mark that tells a reader to take a short breath, the written equivalent of a pause in speech

explanation.surface: Something that makes us hesitate, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gives us pause' reads as an idiom for making someone think twice; literally, this mark makes a reader pause briefly, and 'in a manner of speaking' hints that it marks the rhythm of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: This punctuation mark signals a brief pause between parts of a sentence.

parts.note: 'set' is read as a complete series of items such as stamps, which this hobbyist aims to complete

explanation.surface: A man whose pastime has a fixed aim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set purpose' sounds like determination; it means the hobbyist's goal is to complete a set.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobbyist who gathers stamps, coins or other items is an accumulator of sets.

parts.note: tube-shaped fur coverings that keep the hands warm

explanation.surface: People clasping each other's hands to console one another.
explanation.walkthrough: Holding hands for comfort sounds emotional; here the comfort is warmth, the hands tucked inside a fur tube.
explanation.definitionFit: Fur tubes into which both hands are slipped for warmth.

parts.note: 1 Down is a collector, so this is a collector of patients

explanation.surface: A tolerant hobbyist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patient' looks like the adjective meaning tolerant; it is the noun, and the vehicle collects patients.
explanation.definitionFit: This emergency vehicle picks up sick or injured people.

clue.text: Should an itinerant dentist do this punishment ?

definitions.text: Should an itinerant dentist do this

explanation.surface: A wandering dentist's packing up is likened to a military punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: A travelling dentist would PACK his DRILL before moving on; pack drill is also a military punishment of marching in full kit.
explanation.definitionFit: Pack drill is a soldier's penalty of marching while carrying full equipment; a roaming tooth-doctor would stow his boring tool.

clue.text: Locations including a lot of top people

definitions.note: a lot here is a portion one is allotted, the homes that fall to royalty

indicators.note: including means the word for locations holds the letter inside it

parts.note: places are locations

explanation.surface: Sites that accommodate many important figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' looks like 'many'; 'a' is the letter put inside PLACES and 'lot' is one's share in life.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal residences are where monarchs and grandees live.

parts.note: a yellow sweet sauce linked to the children's taunt cowardy-cowardy

explanation.surface: A golden dessert linked with timidity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cowardy custard' is a British children's taunt for a coward; yellow is also slang for cowardly.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet yellow sauce of milk and eggs, linked with cowards through a playground taunt.

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Someone behaved as his name suggested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lived up to' looks like an idiom; 'up' turns LIVED back to front, giving the name of Satan, who lives up to it.
explanation.definitionFit: The evil one, Satan, is named by the word spelt backwards from lived.

clue.text: In money I have something encouraging

parts.note: taken as written
a cent is a coin, so money
contracted to I've

explanation.surface: Having cash makes me feel hopeful.
explanation.definitionFit: A spur or motivation is a thing that encourages action.

parts.note: a lar is a Roman household god
Ge or Gaia is the Greek goddess of the earth

explanation.surface: A mighty divinity, the goddess of the earth.
explanation.walkthrough: LAR, one of the Roman lares, the household gods, is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Big and sizeable are synonyms of great.

clue.text: They are assumed to prevent that sinking feeling

definitions.text: They are assumed to prevent that sinking feeling

parts.words: They are assumed to prevent that sinking feeling
parts.note: 'assumed' here means put on, and the sinking is literal: buoyancy rings worn to stop someone drowning

explanation.surface: Things we take for granted keep away a sense of dread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assumed' suggests supposed, and 'that sinking feeling' suggests dismay; read literally they are put on so the wearer does not sink in water.
explanation.definitionFit: Buoyant rings worn round the body keep a person afloat in water.

clue.text: It's done for others when he puts his name to I.O.Us.

definitions.text: It's done for others when he puts his name to I.O.Us.

parts.words: It's done for others when he puts his name to I.O.Us.
parts.note: a word meaning done on behalf of others is built from this cleric's title followed by the letters I, O, U, S

explanation.surface: A man signing promissory notes does it on behalf of other people.
explanation.walkthrough: Put the clergyman's title in front of I.O.U.S and you get VICARIOUS, meaning done or felt on behalf of others; 'he' is the clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: A parish priest in the Church of England holds this title.

clue.text: It's under the Board of Education

definitions.text: It's under the Board of Education

parts.words: It's under the Board of Education
parts.note: the 'Board of Education' is read as a classroom blackboard, and this stand holds it up

explanation.surface: An office subordinate to a government education department.
explanation.walkthrough: The Board of Education sounds like an official body; here it is a school blackboard, which rests on a wooden stand.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter's or teacher's three-legged stand supports a board or canvas.

explanation.surface: Someone bold enough to propose a brawl.
explanation.definitionFit: To dare is to defy someone to act, and to offer fight is to call an opponent out; both are senses of the same verb.

clue.text: A number of workers in possession

definitions.note: a phrase describing the people who hold a property, standing for a plural noun

parts.note: ten is a number
worker ants: crosswords often use ants for workers

explanation.surface: Some of the staff are holding something.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: the people 'in possession' of a rented house are its occupants.
explanation.definitionFit: Occupiers who rent a property are the ones holding possession of it.

clue.text: X marks the spot for a political address

definitions.text: X marks the spot for a political address

parts.words: X marks the spot for a political address
parts.note: the Roman numeral X is ten, and the Prime Minister lives at that number in Downing Street

explanation.surface: A ballot cross indicates where a political speech is given.
explanation.walkthrough: X suggests a voting cross and 'address' a speech; X is ten in Roman numerals and the address is the British Prime Minister's house in Downing Street.
explanation.definitionFit: The British Prime Minister's official residence in Downing Street is known by its house number.

indicators.note: to confound is to throw into confusion, so the composer's name with its s is jumbled

parts.note: the composer's name with its possessive s counted as a letter
an aspirate is the breathy h sound, so aspiration gives H

explanation.surface: A frenzied performer upsets the Italian composer's ambitions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aspiration' looks like ambition; in phonetics it is the breathy sound written as the letter H. 'Confounds' scrambles only the composer's name with its s, and the H is added after.
explanation.definitionFit: A whirling Sufi mystic spins ecstatically in worship, hence a wild dancer.

clue.text: They might easily be one's trial

indicators.note: signals that the letters of the following words could readily be rearranged into something else

parts.note: the apostrophe-s counts as a letter here

explanation.surface: Family members can easily be a burden to a person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might easily be' rearranges ONES and TRIAL; the surface's truth, that family can be trying, gives the clue its point.
explanation.definitionFit: Family members are referred to with the pronoun, the clue's whole sense describing them.

clue.text: What it costs Dad to keep Mum ?

definitions.text: What it costs Dad to keep Mum ?

parts.words: What it costs Dad to keep Mum
parts.note: 'Mum' is read as the British word meaning silent, so this is a payment to keep someone quiet

explanation.surface: The price a father pays to support the mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' looks like mother; 'keep mum' means stay silent, so this is a bribe for silence.
explanation.definitionFit: A bribe paid to stop someone revealing a secret.

explanation.surface: Unknown people wearing spectacles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' is British slang for strange, so a 'rummer' is a stranger thing; rummers are also large drinking glasses.
explanation.definitionFit: Odder things, from the slang rum meaning odd, share a spelling with large wine goblets.

clue.text: Fruitless way to raise East European' currency

parts.note: St is short for street, a way

indicators.note: in a down clue raising lifts the letters so they read upwards

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for East
lire, the former Italian money

explanation.surface: A pointless way of increasing a currency from eastern Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East European' looks like one phrase; split it into E plus the lire, and 'to raise' turns ELIRE into ERILE.
explanation.definitionFit: Barren land or creatures bear no fruit or offspring.

explanation.surface: Magicians travelling to a holy shrine.
explanation.walkthrough: A conjurer palms cards or coins, hiding them in the hand; medieval pilgrims to the Holy Land carried palm leaves and were named after them.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleight-of-hand tricksters hide things in the palm, and medieval pilgrims bore palm fronds home from Jerusalem.

parts.note: mortars sound like guns, but here they are grinding bowls used with a club-shaped tool

explanation.surface: Artillery crews firing their mortars.
explanation.walkthrough: Mortars suggest artillery bombarding; here they are kitchen bowls, and the tools pound spices in them.
explanation.definitionFit: Club-shaped tools crush substances inside a bowl.

indicators.note: read as 'sort' a verb, the letters of the next word are sorted into a new order

explanation.surface: A kind of size alienates people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' looks like 'kind of'; it tells you to sort the nine letters of ESTRANGES.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnitude or bigness is a synonym of size.

explanation.surface: Someone stood and put on clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting out of bed and being dressed up in an outfit are both meanings of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: His valedictory sentiments have been voiced by many

definitions.text: His valedictory sentiments have been voiced by many

parts.words: His valedictory sentiments have been voiced by many
parts.note: the Italian composer of the popular song 'Good-bye!', sung by countless singers

explanation.surface: A man's farewell speech has been repeated by many people.
explanation.walkthrough: The Italian songwriter F. Paolo Tosti wrote the famous parlour song 'Good-bye!', so his farewell is sung by many.
explanation.definitionFit: A songwriter of Victorian parlour ballads, the most famous being a farewell song.

clue.text: Symbol shows how to add numbers

parts.note: to tot up is to add
'em is short for them, here the numbers to be added

explanation.surface: An emblem demonstrating how to do sums.
explanation.walkthrough: The instruction 'tot 'em' (add them up) is what 'how to add numbers' shows.
explanation.definitionFit: A carved emblem standing for a clan or family is a sacred symbol.

parts.note: the bar is a musical bar, not a pub, and this word is the speed of the music

explanation.surface: Closing time at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time in the bar' suggests a pub's call for last orders; the bar is a measure of music.
explanation.definitionFit: Musical pace, the speed at which beats in each measure are played.

clue.text: Name given to a bird by us

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
taken as written

explanation.surface: We give a name to a feathered creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman emperor and a book of the Bible bear this name.

parts.note: a refuge for someone who dislikes women would be an island inhabited only by males

explanation.surface: A refuge for people who oppose women's rights.
explanation.walkthrough: The island in the Irish Sea is read literally as an island of men only.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-governing island between Britain and Ireland, its name read as an island of men.

parts.note: the adjective that describes beggars: without money

explanation.surface: A phrase that is beyond words, as in 'beggars description'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beggars description' is the idiom meaning cannot be described; read as a noun phrase, it asks for the word describing beggars.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no money at all is the state of beggars.

indicators.note: madly signals the letters of the two words before it going wild

explanation.surface: Someone asking why a thing is so wildly flashy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Madly' scrambles WHYSO into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Flashy or pretentious behaviour makes a display, the sense of this adjective.
